title: Closed Laugh-O-Gram Films and moved to Hollywood with one unreleased reel
statement: After the Pictorial Clubs distributor bankruptcy left Laugh-O-Gram Films insolvent, Disney filed the Kansas City studio for bankruptcy in July 1923, sold his movie camera, and moved to Hollywood carrying an unfinished reel of Alice's Wonderland as his only asset.
outcome: In October 1923 New York distributor Margaret Winkler contracted six Alice comedies, and Disney and his brother Roy founded the Disney Brothers Studio, the direct predecessor of the Walt Disney Company.

title: Refused Charles Mintz's ultimatum and surrendered Oswald the Lucky Rabbit
statement: Traveling to New York in February 1928 to negotiate a larger Oswald budget, Disney learned that Universal owned the character, that Mintz had signed away most of his animators, and that he must accept a twenty percent cut; he refused the ultimatum and returned to California having lost the series and much of his staff, keeping only Ub Iwerks.
outcome: On the train home Disney resolved to create a new character he would own outright; Mickey Mouse followed within months, and Oswald was eventually traded back to Disney by NBCUniversal in 2006 in exchange for sportscaster Al Michaels' services.

title: Bet on synchronized sound with Steamboat Willie
statement: After two silent Mickey Mouse shorts failed to find a distributor, Disney, having seen The Jazz Singer, produced the third short with a fully post-produced synchronized soundtrack recorded with a click track and Pat Powers' Cinephone system.
outcome: Steamboat Willie became the most popular cartoon of its time and Mickey Mouse's official debut, was selected for the National Film Registry in 1998, and established the studio as the industry's technical leader.

title: Produced Snow White as the first American animated feature
statement: Ignoring warnings from his wife, his brother, and industry insiders who called the project Disney's Folly, Disney committed the studio to a feature-length cartoon announced to The New York Times in June 1934 at an estimated $250,000, ultimately mortgaging his house and borrowing $250,000 from Bank of America to finish a film that cost $1.49 million.
outcome: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs premiered December 21, 1937, earned more than $8 million in its initial release to become the highest-grossing film of 1938, and won Disney an honorary Oscar of one full-sized and seven miniature statuettes, funding the Burbank studio and the golden age that followed.

title: Took the company public to survive the wartime debt crisis
statement: With Pinocchio and Fantasia losing money after European markets closed in 1939 and the studio deeply in debt by February 1941, Disney and Roy started Walt Disney Productions' first public stock offering in 1940 alongside heavy salary cuts.
outcome: The offering kept the studio solvent through the war; the company has remained publicly traded ever since, listed on the New York Stock Exchange and a Dow Jones Industrial Average component since 1991.

title: Signed the ABC television deal to finance Disneyland
statement: After CBS and NBC passed and banks proved unwilling to fund a theme park, Disney signed with ABC on March 29, 1954, creating the Disneyland anthology series in exchange for the network's participation in financing the park through the jointly owned Disneyland, Inc.
outcome: Disneyland opened July 17, 1955, drew 3.6 million guests in its first year, and was wholly owned by Walt Disney Productions by 1960; the ABC relationship culminated in Disney's acquisition of the network in the mid-1990s.

title: Assembled Florida Project land secretly and chartered Reedy Creek
statement: Beginning in April 1964, Disney used dummy corporations with names like Ayefour Corporation and Reedy Creek Ranch to assemble 27,443 acres southwest of Orlando for as little as $100 an acre, delaying deed filings to prevent speculation, and petitioned the Florida legislature for the Reedy Creek Improvement District to govern the property with near-total autonomy.
outcome: The land became Walt Disney World, opened by Roy O. Disney in 1971 and today the most visited vacation resort in the world and the largest single-site employer in the United States; the district Disney chartered in 1967 survived until the state restructured it as the Central Florida Tourism Oversight District in 2023.

title: Founded the California Institute of the Arts
statement: Disney coordinated the 1961 merger of the financially distressed Chouinard Art Institute and the Los Angeles Conservatory of Music into CalArts, the first degree-granting American institution of higher learning created for students of both the visual and performing arts, drawing on the interdisciplinary ideal he had pursued from Fantasia through WED Enterprises.
outcome: CalArts opened its Valencia campus and became the industry's central training ground, with its character animation program and its A113 classroom producing generations of animators who staffed Disney, Pixar, and the wider animation industry.
